chapterNote: Chapter 21 hangs between two declarations of the LORD's sovereignty — He turns the king's heart like a stream wherever He wills (v.1), and no wisdom, plan, or war-horse can prevail against Him (vv.30-31). Between those bookends runs a string of antithetical proverbs contrasting the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the hasty, the generous and the greedy. Two great threads recur: the LORD prizes justice and right doing above ritual sacrifice (vv.3,27), and the tongue, the temper, and the appetite are tested as surely as the heart (vv.2,23). The whole chapter insists that human striving runs only as far as the LORD permits.

1.text: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; He channels it wherever He pleases.
1.amp: The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD like the watercourses [palg — irrigation channels, streams diverted at will]; He turns [natah — bends, redirects] it wherever He delights [chaphets — takes pleasure, freely chooses].
1.notes: natah (H5186) is to bend or turn aside, the image of a farmer cutting an irrigation ditch to send water where he wills; even the heart of the most powerful man on earth is no more resistant to God than a stream is to the hand that channels it (cf. Ezra 6:22; Prov 16:9). chaphets (H2654) marks it as God's free pleasure, not constraint.

2.text: Every road a man walks looks straight to his own eyes, but it is the LORD who weighs the heart.
2.amp: Every way [derek — road, the whole pattern of a life] of a man [ish] is right [yashar — straight, upright] in his own eyes [ayin], but the LORD weighs [takan — measures, gauges] the hearts.
2.notes: takan (H8505) is to weigh or measure with exactness, as on a balance; self-assessment always reads its own road as straight (cf. 16:2; 21:2 nearly repeats it), but the LORD assays the inner motive the man cannot see in himself. yashar (H3477) is the book's word for a life that runs true rather than crooked.

3.text: To do what is right and just is more pleasing to the LORD than sacrifice.
3.amp: To do [asah — perform, carry out in deed] righteousness [tsedaqah — right dealing, righteous acts] and justice [mishpat — right judgment] is more chosen [bachar — preferred, selected] by the LORD than sacrifice [zebach].
3.notes: bachar (H977) means to choose or prefer; the LORD positively prefers ethical obedience to ritual offering (cf. 1 Sam 15:22; Hos 6:6; Mic 6:6-8). tsedaqah (H6666) and mishpat (H4941) are the paired social virtues — right relating and right deciding — that worship without obedience cannot replace.

4.text: Haughty eyes and a swollen heart — the very lamp by which the wicked live — is sin.
4.amp: A high [rum — lifted up, lofty] look [ayin — eyes], and a proud [rachab — wide, broad, swollen] heart, and the lamp [niyr — the lamp, the night-light, or 'tillage'] of the wicked [rasha], is sin [chattath].
4.notes: the Hebrew niyr (H5215) can mean either a freshly-plowed field or a lamp; reading it as 'lamp' (so WEB) makes the whole inner life and guiding light of the wicked sin at its root. rachab (H7342), literally 'wide,' pictures a heart puffed and swollen with self — pride is not a stray fault but the very flame they steer by.

5.text: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes surely to want.
5.amp: The thoughts [machashabah — plans, calculated purposes] of the diligent [charuts — sharp, decisive, industrious] tend only to plenty [mothar — profit, advantage]; but everyone who is hasty [uts — presses, rushes headlong] only to want.
5.notes: uts (H213) is to press or hurry impatiently — the opposite of the diligent man's measured machashabah (H4284), his careful plan. Proverbs prizes thoughtful steadiness over impulsive speed; the rusher reaps lack as surely as the planner reaps gain (cf. 19:2; 28:20).

6.text: Treasure won by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor, a snare for those who chase after death.
6.amp: The getting of treasures [otsar] by a lying [sheqer — false, deceitful] tongue [lashon] is a vanity [hebel — a breath, a vapor] driven to and fro by those who seek [baqash — pursue] death [mavet].
6.notes: hebel (H1892) is the 'vapor, breath' word that drums through Ecclesiastes — wealth gained by deceit evaporates as quickly as breath on a cold morning. sheqer (H8267) is falsehood; the deceiver imagines he is chasing riches, but he is really hunting his own mavet (H4194), death (cf. 10:2; 13:11).

7.text: The violence of the wicked will drag them away, because they refuse to do what is just.
7.amp: The robbery [shod — violence, devastation, plunder] of the wicked [rasha] shall drag them off [garar — drag away, sweep along], because they refuse [maen — decline, say no] to do [asah] justice [mishpat].
7.notes: garar (H1641) is to drag or sweep away, as a flood drags off what stands in its path; the wicked man's own violence becomes the current that carries him to ruin. The cause is named flatly: a settled refusal (maen, H3985) to practice mishpat — justice — the very thing the LORD prefers to sacrifice (v.3).

8.text: The way of a guilt-laden man is twisted and strange, but the conduct of the pure is straight.
8.amp: The way [derek] of a man [ish] is crooked [haphakpak — twisted, devious, full of turns] and strange; but as for the pure [zak — clean, clear, transparent], his work [poal — deed, conduct] is upright [yashar].
8.notes: haphakpak (H2019) is an intensive, doubled form — 'twisty-turny,' a way that doubles back on itself; the guilty man's path bends to hide his guilt. zak (H2134) means transparent, clear as clean water — the pure man has nothing to bend around, so his poal (H6467) runs straight and yashar (H3477).

9.text: Better to live in a corner of the rooftop than to share a whole house with a quarrelsome wife.
9.amp: It is better [tov] to dwell [yashab — sit, settle] in a corner of the housetop, than with a contentious [madon — strife, quarreling] woman [ishshah] in a house [bayith] shared in common.
9.notes: madon (H4066) is contention, the endless wrangling that poisons a home. The picture is vivid: a cramped, exposed corner of the flat Middle-Eastern roof is preferable to a spacious house if peace is gone from it (the verse is repeated almost exactly at 25:24; cf. 21:19).

10.text: The soul of the wicked craves evil; his own neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.
10.amp: The soul [nephesh — the appetite, the inner self] of the wicked [rasha] desires [avah — longs for, craves] evil [ra]; his neighbor [rea — friend, fellow] finds no favor [chanan — grace, mercy] in his eyes.
10.notes: avah (H183) is deep craving, the appetite of the nephesh (H5315) itself; wickedness is not a slip but a hunger. Where the heart's appetite is set on ra (H7451), even the nearest rea (H7453) — friend, neighbor — receives no chanan (H2603), no pity. Cruelty flows from a soul that loves evil.

11.text: When the mocker is punished, the simple grows wiser; when the wise is instructed, he takes in knowledge.
11.amp: When the scorner [luts — mocker, scoffer] is punished [anash — fined, penalized], the simple [peti — naive, easily-led] is made wise [chakam]; and when the wise [chakam] is instructed [sakal — given insight], he receives [laqach — takes in, lays hold of] knowledge [daat].
11.notes: two ways to learn: the peti (H6612) learns by watching the mocker pay his fine (anash, H6064), while the chakam (H2450) learns by direct instruction. The simple needs the spectacle of judgment; the wise needs only a word (cf. 19:25). laqach (H3947) is to take and keep — the wise man seizes knowledge offered.

12.text: The Righteous One marks the house of the wicked and brings the wicked down to ruin.
12.amp: The righteous one [tsaddiq] wisely considers [sakal — observes with insight] the house [bayith] of the wicked [rasha]; God overthrows [salaph — twists down, overturns] the wicked for their wickedness [ra].
12.notes: many read 'the Righteous One' as God Himself, who watches (sakal, H7919) the household of the wicked and then topples it (salaph, H5557, to overturn). The wicked may seem secure in their bayith (H1004), but a watching Justice notes their evil and brings the whole house down (cf. Ps 37:35-36).

13.text: Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry out one day and not be answered.
13.amp: Whoever stops [atam — closes, plugs] his ears [ozen] at the cry [zeaqah — outcry, shriek of distress] of the poor [dal — weak, low, helpless], he also shall cry [qara — call out] himself, but shall not be answered [anah — responded to].
13.notes: atam (H331) is to shut tight, deliberately plug the ear; the zeaqah (H2201) is the desperate outcry of the dal (H1800), the weak. The justice is exact and reciprocal — the ear closed to the poor will find heaven's ear closed to it (cf. 28:27; Matt 18:23-35; Jas 2:13).

14.text: A gift given in secret soothes anger, and a bribe slipped into the cloak calms fierce wrath.
14.amp: A gift [mattan — a present freely given] in secret [sether — hidden, concealed] pacifies [kaphah — subdues, quiets] anger [aph — the flaring nostril, hot anger]; and a bribe [shochad] in the bosom [cheq — the lap, the fold of the garment] calms strong wrath [chemah — burning fury].
14.notes: aph (H639) is literally the 'nose, nostril,' anger pictured as flared and snorting; chemah (H2534) is hotter still, fury like venom. The proverb observes, without simply commending, how a quiet gift cools rage — but the parallel word shochad (H7810), bribe, leaves the moral edge sharp: the same act may be peacemaking or corruption depending on the heart.

15.text: When justice is done, it is joy to the righteous, but terror to those who work iniquity.
15.amp: It is joy [simchah — gladness, rejoicing] to the just [tsaddiq] to do [asah] justice [mishpat]; but ruin [mechittah — destruction, dismay, terror] to the workers [paal — doers] of iniquity [aven].
15.notes: the same event — justice carried out — lands as simchah (H8057), gladness, on the tsaddiq (H6662) and as mechittah (H4288), dismay and ruin, on the worker of aven (H205). One delights to see right done; the other dreads it, because justice is his undoing (cf. 10:29).

16.text: The man who strays from the road of understanding will come to rest in the assembly of the dead.
16.amp: The man [adam] who wanders [taah — strays, goes astray] out of the way [derek] of understanding [sakal — prudence, insight] shall remain [nuach — settle, come to rest] in the congregation [qahal — assembly] of the dead [repha — the shades, departed spirits].
16.notes: taah (H8582) is to wander off like a lost sheep; the man who strays from the way of insight does not merely lose his bearings but ends, with grim irony, 'at rest' (nuach, H5117) — among the repaim (H7496), the shades in the assembly of the dead. To leave wisdom's road is to walk toward the grave (cf. 2:18-19; 9:18).

17.text: He who loves pleasure will become a poor man; whoever loves wine and oil will never grow rich.
17.amp: He who loves [ahab — delights in, is devoted to] pleasure [simchah — merriment, indulgence] shall be a poor man [machsor — in want, lacking]; he who loves wine [yayin] and oil [shemen — olive oil, the mark of luxury] shall not be rich [ashar].
17.notes: ahab (H157) is wholehearted love; the danger is not wine or oil themselves but loving them — making the feast (simchah, here used of revelry) the aim of life. Such devotion to indulgence drains a man to want (cf. 23:21). Wine and oil were the staples of celebration and wealth; chasing them as ends impoverishes.

18.text: The wicked becomes a ransom for the righteous, and the treacherous takes the place of the upright.
18.amp: The wicked [rasha] shall be a ransom [kopher — ransom price, atonement payment] for the righteous [tsaddiq], and the transgressor [bagad — the treacherous, faithless] for the upright [yashar].
18.notes: kopher (H3724) is the price paid to redeem a life; in the outworking of providence the calamity the wicked plotted falls back on themselves and so spares the righteous — the trap meant for the upright catches the one who set it (cf. 11:8; Esther 7:10). bagad (H898) names the betrayer, who ends up paying for the very man he meant to harm.

19.text: Better to live alone in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and bad-tempered wife.
19.amp: It is better [tov] to dwell [yashab] in the wilderness [midbar — desert, uninhabited waste], than with a contentious [madon — strife] and fretful [kaas — vexation, ill temper, provocation] woman [ishshah].
19.notes: an intensified echo of v.9: now the alternative is not a cramped rooftop but the empty midbar (H4057), a barren desert — still preferable to a home filled with madon (H4066) and kaas (H3708), strife and constant irritation. The hyperbole presses the point that peace, not comfort, makes a dwelling livable.

20.text: Precious treasure and oil are stored in the home of the wise, but a fool gulps down all he has.
20.amp: There is treasure [otsar] to be desired [chamad — precious, delighted in] and oil [shemen] in the dwelling [naveh — habitation, pasture-home] of the wise [chakam]; but a foolish [kesil — dull, stupid fool] man [adam] swallows it up [bala — gulps down, devours].
20.notes: the wise man's naveh (H5116) holds stored otsar (H214) and shemen — the reserves of prudence and provision — while the kesil (H3684) bala (H1104), swallows his down whole, consuming today what should provide for tomorrow. The contrast is between the saver and the squanderer (cf. v.17; Luke 15:13).

21.text: Whoever pursues righteousness and steadfast love finds life, righteousness, and honor.
21.amp: He who follows [radaph — pursues, chases hard] after righteousness [tsedaqah] and mercy [chesed — steadfast love, covenant loyalty] finds [matsa — attains, discovers] life [chay], righteousness [tsedaqah], and honor [kabod — glory, weight].
21.notes: radaph (H7291) is the hunter's word, to pursue relentlessly — and what is pursued is not gain but tsedaqah (H6666) and chesed (H2617), right dealing and loyal love. The reward circles back to include tsedaqah itself: the one who chases righteousness finds it, plus life and kabod (H3519), the 'weight' of true honor (cf. Matt 6:33).

22.text: A wise man scales the city of warriors and brings down the stronghold in which it trusted.
22.amp: A wise [chakam] man scales [alah — goes up, mounts] the city [ir] of the mighty [gibbor — warriors, the strong], and casts down [yarad — brings down] the strength [oz — might, fortress-power] of its confidence [mivtach — the thing it trusts in].
22.notes: wisdom outdoes raw force: one chakam (H2450) scales (alah, H5927) a fortified ir defended by gibborim (H1368), mighty men, and topples the oz (H5797) — the fortified strength — in which they put their mivtach (H4009), their trust. Counsel breaches walls that armies cannot (cf. Eccl 9:14-16; Prov 24:5).

23.text: Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from trouble.
23.amp: Whoever keeps [shamar — guards, watches over] his mouth [peh] and his tongue [lashon] keeps [shamar] his soul [nephesh] from troubles [tsarah — distress, tribulation].
23.notes: the doubled shamar (H8104) ties the guarding of speech directly to the guarding of the self: the man who stands sentry over his peh (H6310) and lashon (H3956) spares his nephesh (H5315) the tsarah (H6869), the tight straits, that loose words invite (cf. 13:3; Jas 3:2-6).

24.text: Proud, arrogant, 'Mocker' is his name — the man who acts in overflowing insolence.
24.amp: Proud [zed — insolent, presumptuous] and haughty [yahir — arrogant, high-minded] scorner [luts — mocker] is his name [shem — name, reputation], who acts [asah] in the arrogance [zadon — presumption, insolence] of pride.
24.notes: the verse piles up the vocabulary of pride — zed (H2086), yahir (H3093), luts (H3887), zadon (H2087) — to portray a single character whose very shem (H8034), his reputation, is 'Mocker.' His scoffing is no occasional fault but the settled style of a life governed by overflowing self-importance (cf. 1:22; 9:7-8).

25.text: The craving of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to do any work.
25.amp: The desire [taavah — longing, craving] of the slothful [atsel — sluggard, lazy one] kills [muth — puts to death] him; for his hands refuse [maen — decline] to labor [asah — to work, to do].
25.notes: the cruel irony: the sluggard is not killed by overwork but by his own taavah (H8378) — he craves what he will not lift a hand to gain. atsel (H6102) is Proverbs' lazy man; his appetite is real but his hands maen (H3985), refuse, so the very desire that should drive him instead destroys (muth, H4191) him (cf. 13:4; 26:13-16).

26.text: All day long the greedy man keeps craving, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.
26.amp: He covets [avah — craves, longs] greedily [taavah — with longing] all the day [yom] long; but the righteous [tsaddiq] gives [natan] and spares [chasak — withholds, holds back] not.
26.notes: set against the sluggard of v.25, this verse contrasts two appetites: the greedy man's nonstop avah (H183) and taavah (H8378), craving that only takes, against the tsaddiq (H6662) who natan (H5414), gives, and does not chasak (H2820), does not hold back. Open-handed generosity is the very signature of the righteous (cf. v.13; Ps 37:21,26).

27.text: The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable — how much more when he brings it with vile intent.
27.amp: The sacrifice [zebach] of the wicked [rasha] is an abomination [toebah — a detestable, loathsome thing]; how much more, when he brings [bo — carries in, offers] it with a wicked mind [zimmah — evil scheme, depravity]?
27.notes: echoing v.3, this verse turns to worship: even the wicked man's zebach (H2077), his offering, is toebah (H8441), an abomination to God — and worse still when he brings it as a cover for zimmah (H2154), a calculated evil purpose. Ritual cannot launder a corrupt heart; it deepens the offense (cf. 15:8; Isa 1:11-15).

28.text: A lying witness will perish, but the man who truly listens will speak on and endure.
28.amp: A false witness [ed kazab — a witness of lies] shall perish [abad — be destroyed, vanish]; but the man [ish] that hears [shama — listens, heeds] shall speak [dabar] for ever [netsach — perpetuity, enduring victory].
28.notes: kazab (H3577) is falsehood; the false witness abad (H6), perishes, his testimony swept away. By contrast the man who truly shama (H8085), listens before he speaks, will dabar (H1696) lanetsach (H5331) — speak enduringly, his word standing the test of time. Truth heard and carefully spoken outlasts the lie (cf. 12:19; 19:9).

29.text: A wicked man puts on a brazen face, but the upright gives careful thought to his way.
29.amp: A wicked [rasha] man [ish] hardens [azaz — makes strong, brazen, defiant] his face [panim]; but as for the upright [yashar], he establishes [kun — makes firm, directs] his way [derek].
29.notes: the contrast is between bluster and consideration: the rasha (H7563) azaz (H5810) his panim (H6440) — stiffens his face into a defiant mask to push his way through — while the yashar (H3477) attends to and kun (H3559), establishes, his actual derek (H1870). One projects confidence; the other secures the road he walks (the Qere reads 'considers his way').

30.text: There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can stand against the LORD.
30.amp: There is no wisdom [chokmah] nor understanding [tebunah — discernment, insight] nor counsel [etsah — plan, scheme] against the LORD [YHWH].
30.notes: the chapter's closing bookend (with v.1 and v.31): the three highest human faculties — chokmah (H2451), tebunah (H8394), etsah (H6098) — are named only to be canceled, for none can be marshaled 'against' (neged) the LORD. Every plan that opposes Him is doomed before it begins (cf. Ps 33:10-11; Isa 8:10; Acts 5:39).

31.text: Though the war-horse stands harnessed and waiting for the hour of battle, it is the LORD alone who grants deliverance.
31.amp: The horse [sus] is prepared [kun — made ready, equipped] for the day [yom] of battle [milchamah — war, combat]; but safety [teshuah — deliverance, victory] is of the LORD [YHWH].
31.notes: kun (H3559), the same 'establish' verb as v.29, here means to equip: man does his diligent part, readying the war-horse for milchamah (H4421). Yet the teshuah (H8668) — the deliverance, the win — belongs to the LORD alone. Human preparation is right and required, but the outcome rests entirely in God's hand (cf. Ps 20:7; 33:17; Prov 16:9).
